title: Emmett Hardy, Abbie Brunies, instrument preference and sign-off
summary: He talks about Emmett Hardy and Abbie Brunies, says he prefers clarinet to saxophone, and the interview closes.

story.theme_name: Thanks and goodbyes: closing the interview
story.community_name: Closing the interview: thanks, goodbyes and tape running out

blocks.x: Well, I think him and Big Spine are back. Is that so? Did you ever play with Big? No, I've never played with him. Did you ever hear him? Yeah, yeah, yeah. They always said that he tried to imitate Emmett. Is that right? Yeah, that's right. That's right. Emmett was quite young, didn't he? He did, yes. Did you ever play with Emmett? Yes, I played with him. Which band, any particular? Well, no, I'll tell you, quite a few times he played some extra jobs that Abby Brunner couldn't make out at the halfway house. By the way, I wanted to ask you, did Abby and Georgie ever play together? Oh, yes. In the same band? Yes. Did you ever see them when they were kids? They used to play a French horn, too. Yeah, Georgie used to play what they call alto. Yeah, yeah. Yeah, he used to play in the parades. Yeah, yeah. Abby used to play the trumpet. Old Abby played a real good trumpet. I used to like his trumpet playing. Your style is very much like Bix, too, at times. Yeah, yeah. Abby used to get a very good tone out of a trumpet. Very good. Clean, clean trumpet player. Very good. Charlie, what do you prefer playing, clarinet or saxophone? Oh, clarinet, Doctor. You still like it better? Yeah. I was on the impression you liked sax. No, I still... You do it because it's more commercial, is that it? That's it, Doctor. Yeah. But your first love, you still love it? Still like the old clown. Do you like any other system better than the alibi? No. No, I don't. What's the weather? Thank you so much. And this is May the 17th, 1952. And we're speaking to you from New Orleans, Louisiana. It's an informal interview between Dr. Admiral Suchar interviewing Charlie Cordella of the great halfway house in the audience rhythm. Thank you for listening. Tell them goodbye, Charlie. Bye-bye, folks. Bye-bye, folks.
